turns.t: Quick one, doctor, I've another appointment at the optician. It's my hearing aids. I can't hear the television, even with them in, and my wife says I've got it up so loud the neighbours complain.
I'll be quick, but let's get this right. Which ear is worse?
Both, really. The left a bit more. I've had the aids for about four years. ~
When did you last have them checked? ~
Two years ago, at the hospital. They said the hearing was a bit worse, and adjusted the settings. ~
Are they working, do you think, or has something changed? ~
They whistle sometimes, and the batteries, I've been changing them every four days. ~
That's worth checking. Four days is short. ~
That's what I thought. ~
Tell me about your general health. Anything long-term?
Only the hearing loss. I'm seventy-three, you know.
Let me check your pulse and blood pressure quickly. Pulse 72, blood pressure 130 over 80.
Normal for my age? ~
Very good. Now, I'd like to explain how I'd approach this. First, the hearing aids themselves. They can get clogged with wax, and the tubes can go stiff. ~
Right. ~
Second, wax in the ear canal can block sound, and make the aids whistle. ~
I haven't had my ears cleaned in years. ~
Third, the batteries. If they run out that quickly, there may be a problem with the aid itself. ~
Can you fix it? ~
Not here, but the audiology department can. I'll write to them with what you've told me. ~
How long will that take? ~
A couple of weeks for the appointment. In the meantime, keep the aids dry, and wipe them each night.
I do that already. ~
Good. Don't use cotton buds in your ears, either, it pushes the wax deeper.
I've never used them. ~
Good. Keep the television at a level your wife can tolerate. ~
Ha. That's a tall order. ~
Use subtitles, they help enormously. ~
My daughter said the same. ~
Sensible daughter. Anything else? ~
No, I must dash. Thanks, doctor. ~
Bye. ~
Bye. ~
